James.text: It's the same name as Jacob, which turned into James via the Latin Iacomus and Old French.
James.evidence: James is a modern descendant of the Hebrew name Ya'akov, in English: Jacob. The Hebrew name went successively through the Latin form Iacobus, its derivative Vulgar Latin version Iacomus ... and finally the Old French James.

Michael.text: It was the top US boys' name every year from 1954 to 1998, except 1960, when David beat it.
Michael.evidence: In the United States, Michael was the most popular name of the 20th century, ranking No. 1 from 1954 to 1998 (with the exception of 1960, when it was second to David).

John.text: Jack began as a nickname for John, and was the top boys' name in England and Wales every year from 1995 to 2005.
John.evidence: By contrast Jack, which was a nickname for John but is now established as a name in its own right, was the most popular name given to newborn boys in England and Wales every year from 1995 to 2005.

Robert.text: Rupert is the same name: both come from old Germanic words for "fame" and "bright".
Robert.evidence: The name Robert is an ancient Germanic given name, from Proto-Germanic *Hrōþi- "fame" and *berhta- "bright" ... Another commonly used form of the name is Rupert.

David.text: It means "beloved", from a Hebrew root that originally meant "to boil".
David.evidence: David means 'beloved', derived from the root dôwd, which originally meant 'to boil', but survives in Biblical Hebrew only in the figurative usage 'to love'

William.text: It joins old Germanic words for "will" and "helmet", and took off in England after the Norman conquest.
William.evidence: William is a masculine given name of Germanic origin. It became popular in England after the Norman conquest in 1066 ... The Proto-Germanic name is a compound of *wiljô "will, wish, desire" and *helmaz "helm, helmet".

Richard.text: A top-five boys' name in the 1930s and 1940s, it has dropped out of the top 200 in the 2020s.
Richard.evidence: Rank table, Richard: 1920s 8, 1930s 5, 1940s 5, 1950s 7, ... 2010s 146, 2020s - (a dash means not in top 200 names).

Joseph.text: Genesis explains it twice: "God hath taken away my reproach" and "The LORD shall add to me another son".
Joseph.evidence: The Bible offers two explanations for the origins of the name Yosef: first, it is compared to the word asaf from the root /'sp/, 'taken away': "And she conceived, and bore a son; and said, God hath taken away my reproach"; Yosef is then identified with the similar root /ysp/, meaning 'add': "And she called his name Joseph; and said, The LORD shall add to me another son."

Thomas.text: It started as a nickname: Thomas comes from a Semitic word meaning "twin".
Thomas.evidence: The name Thomas is thus a Greek transliteration of a Semitic epithet meaning "twin".

Christopher.text: Not even in the top 200 in the 1930s, it was the second most popular boys' name in the 1970s, 1980s and 1990s.
Christopher.evidence: Rank table, Christopher: 1880s 177, 1890s-1930s -, 1940s 147, 1950s 49, 1960s 20, 1970s 2, 1980s 2, 1990s 2 (a dash means not in top 200 names).
